videos.title: The Day Japan Lost 4 Aircraft Carriers in Six Minutes
videos.description:
The Day Japan Lost 4 Aircraft Carriers in Six Minutes

June 4, 1942. Midway. The Japanese fleet that hit Pearl Harbor six months ago is hunting for a decisive victory. Four fleet carriers — Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, Hiryu — the backbone of Japan's naval power. The Americans have broken the codes and are waiting. At 10:22 AM, American dive bombers drop out of the clouds and hit three carriers simultaneously. All three are burning within six minutes. Hiryu is sunk by evening. In one morning, Japan loses the war it started. The pilots, the aircraft, the carriers — irreplaceable. Every battle after Midway is a retreat. Six minutes is all it took.

videos.title: The Night 1,000 Bombers Hit Germany for the First Time
videos.description:
The Night 1,000 Bombers Hit Germany for the First Time

May 30, 1942. RAF Bomber Command sends 1,047 aircraft over Cologne in a single night. Nothing like this has ever been attempted. Every available plane — frontline bombers, training aircraft, reserves — is thrown into the sky. For ninety minutes, wave after wave drops incendiaries and high explosives across the city. 600 acres burn. 45,000 people lose their homes in one night. For the first time in the war, Germany feels what the Blitz felt like — but worse. This is the story of Operation Millennium, the raid that proved strategic bombing could break a nation.

videos.title: Why Germany Believed Britain Would Beg for Terms by Autumn
videos.description:
WW2, from the records. https://warshelf.com/

Summer 1940. The logic in Berlin is sound. France is gone in six weeks. Britain's army has just been rescued from Dunkirk without its weapons. The Luftwaffe controls the Channel. The U-boats are tightening around the Atlantic supply lines. Every professional military assessment says Britain has perhaps three months before the arithmetic becomes undeniable. Hitler is so confident Churchill will negotiate that he delays the invasion planning, certain the call is coming. It doesn't come in July. It doesn't come in August. September arrives and the RAF is still up, still fighting, losing aircraft faster than seems sustainable and somehow sustaining it. The German timetable starts to slip. The weather window for invasion closes. The Luftwaffe switches to bombing cities to break civilian morale — and instead hardens it. By October, Berlin's autumn deadline has passed and Britain is still in the war. Germany never produces a satisfactory explanation for why. Because the real answer is that they had studied Britain's strength and completely missed its character.

videos.title: The Night 2 American Submarines Ambushed Japan's Entire Flagship Fleet
videos.description:
The Night 2 American Submarines Ambushed Japan's Entire Flagship Fleet

October 23, 1944. Admiral Kurita's Centre Force is the most powerful surface fleet Japan has assembled since Midway — five battleships, twelve cruisers, fifteen destroyers, steaming through Palawan Passage toward Leyte Gulf. USS Darter and USS Dace find them in the dark. Two submarines against the mightiest fleet Japan has left. They attack anyway. Darter puts four torpedoes into the Atago — Kurita's own flagship — and two more into the Takao. Dace hits the Maya simultaneously. The Atago sinks in eighteen minutes. Kurita goes into the water and has to be pulled out by a destroyer. The Maya disappears in four minutes. In a single night attack, two submarines have sunk two heavy cruisers, crippled a third, and forced the commander of the entire operation to transfer his flag while soaking wet. Kurita reaches Leyte Gulf shaken, his force already diminished, the battle not yet begun.

videos.title: What Tokyo Said When Nagasaki Stopped Responding
videos.description:
What Tokyo Said When Nagasaki Stopped Responding

August 9, 1945. Three days after Hiroshima. Tokyo is still arguing about whether to surrender. Then Nagasaki goes silent. Same pattern. No radio. No telegraph. A second city — gone. The hardliners who swore the Americans only had one bomb have nothing left to say. The war council deadlocks again. It takes the Emperor to break the silence and end the war. Two cities erased in 72 hours. Japan has no response left.

videos.title: What Berlin Said When the 6th Army Stopped Responding from Stalingrad
videos.description:
What Berlin Said When the 6th Army Stopped Responding from Stalingrad

What Berlin Said When the 6th Army Stopped Responding from Stalingrad
January 1943. For weeks, the transmissions from Stalingrad have been getting worse. Desperate. Hungry. Then they stop. 300,000 men — an entire army — goes quiet. Berlin sends message after message. Nothing. The 6th Army, the pride of the Wehrmacht, the force that took Paris, has been swallowed by the frozen ruins of a city they were never supposed to die in. When the silence is finally broken, it's not a German voice. It's a Soviet one. Paulus has surrendered. The army is gone.

videos.title: The Day America Sank Japan's Mightiest Battleship in 5 Hours
videos.description:
The Day America Sank Japan's Mightiest Battleship in 5 Hours

April 7, 1945. The Yamato is the most powerful battleship ever built. Guns large enough to hit a target 26 miles away. Armor thick enough to shrug off almost anything the war has produced. Japan sends her north toward Okinawa with one order: find the American fleet and fight until she sinks. She never gets close. American scouts find her within hours of leaving port. The first wave of aircraft arrives at 12:32. Then the second. Then the third. The Yamato shoots back with everything — her massive guns, her anti-aircraft batteries, everything she has. It makes no difference. By 14:23, less than two hours after the first bomb hits, she rolls onto her side. The forward magazine ignites. The explosion is heard 200 miles away. The mightiest warship Japan ever built lasts five hours against an enemy she was designed to destroy. 2,498 men go down with her. The Americans lose ten aircraft.

videos.title: The Day America Hunted Down Japan's Greatest Admiral
videos.description:
The Day America Hunted Down the Man Who Planned Pearl Harbor

April 18, 1943. American codebreakers intercept a message. Admiral Yamamoto — the man who planned Pearl Harbor, who sent the carriers, who gave the order — is flying an inspection tour over the Pacific. His exact route. His exact schedule. His exact arrival time. The information lands on Roosevelt's desk. The question isn't whether to act. It's whether America can pull it off. Eighteen P-38 Lightnings take off from Guadalcanal, fly 400 miles at wave height to avoid radar, and arrive over the jungle of Bougainville at precisely the right moment. Yamamoto's transport drops out of the sky into the jungle below. The most important admiral in the Imperial Japanese Navy is found dead in the wreckage, still strapped to his seat, white-gloved hand on his sword. The man who woke the sleeping giant doesn't live to see what it does next.

videos.title: The Day American Battleships Shelled Japan's Homeland
videos.description:
The Day American Battleships Shelled Japan's Homeland

February 1945. Task Force 58 — the most powerful carrier fleet ever assembled — closes to within 60 miles of Tokyo. Not to drop a few bombs and escape like Doolittle. To stay. Sixteen carriers, eight battleships, seventeen cruisers. The battleships move in and open fire on the Japanese coast directly — the first time enemy guns have fired on the home islands since the Mongol invasions of the 13th century. The aircraft hit the Nakajima aircraft factories outside Tokyo, the airfields, the industrial targets Japan believed were beyond reach. The Japanese interceptors that come up are overwhelmed. For two days, American ships operate freely in waters Japan considered its own backyard. The psychological damage outlasts the physical. If a fleet this size can sit off Tokyo in February 1945, the question is no longer whether Japan can win. It's whether anything can stop what's coming.

videos.title: What Japan Hid From Its Own People After Midway
videos.description:
What Japan Hid From Its Own People After Midway

June 1942. Four aircraft carriers sunk. 3,000 men dead. The most catastrophic naval defeat in Japanese history. The Japanese public is told none of it. The government announces a great victory in the Central Pacific. Newspapers print celebrations. The few survivors pulled from the water are immediately quarantined — separated from their families, forbidden from writing letters, forbidden from speaking about what they witnessed. Officers who know the truth are transferred to distant postings where they cannot talk. The wounded are treated in sealed hospital wards, away from the general population. When the bodies of senior pilots are quietly returned home, the families are instructed to say nothing. For months, Japan builds its entire strategic picture on a lie so complete that even some members of the government don't know the full scale of what happened. The consequence is devastating — because Japan's next moves are planned as if Midway never occurred. By the time the truth filters through the system, the war has moved on. And there is no recovering what was lost at Midway. There never was.
